text: Worked Example: Permutation GA on a 7-City TSP Goal: minimize tour length (return to start) Cities: {A, B, C , D, E , F , G} Chromosome (permutation): π = [π1, π2, . . . , π7] L(π) = 6∑ k=1 d(πk , πk+1) + d(π7, π1) We will demonstrate one generation: ▶ Evaluate fitness (tour length) ▶ Tournament selection ▶ PMX crossover (step-by-step) ▶ Swap mutation ▶ Replacement with elitism A B C DE F G tour = permutation + return Note Permutation GA requires permutation-aware crossover (PMX). 52 / 73 Distance Data (Example Instance) Symmetric distance matrix (units arbitrary) A B C D E F G A 0 4 3 7 3 6 8 B 4 0 4 6 7 3 5 C 3 4 0 5 6 7 4 D 7 6 5 0 2 4 3 E 3 7 6 2 0 5 6 F 6 3 7 4 5 0 4 G 8 5 4 3 6 4 0 Encoding for PMX A = 1, B = 2, C = 3, D = 4, E = 5, F = 6, G = 7 Fitness L(π) Objetive minimize L(π) Note TSP fitness is a sum along the permutation edges. 53 / 73 Initialization: Population (Size 4) + Fitness Population P (0) (minimize L(π)) ▶ P1 : [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] L = 32 ▶ P2 : [1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 7, 6] L = 29 ▶ P3 : [2, 6, 4, 5, 1, 3, 7] L = 24 ← best ▶ P4 : [3, 1, 5, 2, 7, 4, 6] L = 32 Note Lower tour length = better fitness (minimization). Best tour P3 2 6 4 5 1 3 7 L = 24 Permutation (no repeats) 54 / 73 Selection: Tournament (Size 2) — Visual Assume two tournaments: ▶ Tournament A: P3 vs P1 ⇒ winner P3 ▶ Tournament B: P2 vs P4 ⇒ winner P2 So parents are: Parent 1 = P3 = [2, 6, 4, 5, 1, 3, 7] Parent 2 = P2 = [1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 7, 6] Note Selection biases toward short tours, but keeps diversity. Tournament A P3 L = 24 P1 L = 32 Parent 1 Tournament B P2 L = 29 P4 L = 32 Parent 2 55 / 73 PMX Step 1: Choose Cut Points and Mark Segments Choose cut points c1 = 3, c2 = 5 Parent 1 (P3) 2 6 4 5 1 3 7 Parent 2 (P2) 1 3 2 5 4 7 6 c1 c2 segment copied to child Note PMX copies a contiguous segment (positions) from Parent 1. 56 / 73 PMX Step 2: Copy Segment to Child + Build the Mapping Copy the segment from P1 (positions 3..5) into the child: C = [ , , 4, 5, 1 , , , , ] Build the PMX mapping from the swapped blocks (value-to-value): P1[3..5] = [4, 5, 1], P2[3..5] = [2, 5, 4] M : 4 ↔ 2, 1 ↔ 4 (5 ↔ 5 is trivial and can be ignored.) Note The copied segment fixes positions; the segment pairs define the repair mapping. Swapped blocks (pos 3..5) P1 4 5 1 P2 2 5 4 Mapping M 4 ↔ 2 1 ↔ 4 ignore 5 ↔ 5 How it is used (repair intuition): ▶ When we try to place a value from P2 outside the segment, ▶ if it duplicates something already in the child, ▶ we follow the mapping M (possibly chaining) until we get a value not in the segment. 57 / 73 PMX Step 3: Fill Remaining Positions from Parent 2 (with Repair) Child after copy: C = [ , , 4, 5, 1, , ] Copied set S = {4, 5, 1}. Now fill positions 1, 2, 6, 7 from Parent 2: [1, 3, , , , 7, 6] Key conflict (example at pos 1): ▶ try 1 ⇒ conflict (1 ∈ S) ▶ map 1 → 4 (still conflict) ▶ map 4 → 2 (safe) ⇒ place 2 Then place remaining safe values in order: C = [2, 3, 4, 5, 1, 7, 6] Note Fill from Parent 2, repairing conflicts by chasing the segment map. 1 4 2 1 → 4 4 → 2 conflict conflict safe Child 2 3 4 5 1 7 6 58 / 73 Mutation: Swap Two Positions (Optional Diversification) Assume swap mutation triggers once. Before mutation: C = [2, 3, 4, 5, 1, 7, 6] Swap positions 2 and 6: C ′ = [2, 7, 4, 5, 1, 3, 6] Interpretation (letters): [B, G, D, E , A, C , F ] Note Swap mutation preserves permutation feasibility and injects diversity. swap(2,6) before 2 3 4 5 1 7 6 after 2 7 4 5 1 3 6 59 / 73 Offspring Fitness + Replacement (Elitism) Evaluate mutated offspring C ′: C ′ = [2, 7, 4, 5, 1, 3, 6] ⇒ L(C ′) = 26 Elitist replacement (keep best 1): Keep P3 (L = 24) Then fill remaining slots with best available: {P3(24), C ′(26), P2(29), P1(32)} Drop worst: P4(32). Note Elitism prevents losing the best tour while still exploring via offspring. Next population elite: P3 (24) offspring: C ′ (26) P2 (29) P1 (32) drop: P4 (32) 60 / 73
